sentences.text: Temnodontosaurus is generally estimated to be 9 meters long, making it one of the largest known ichthyosaurs, though not as large as Triassic giants like Shonisaurus or Ichthyotitan. Specimens of T. platyodon, T. trigonodon, and T. crassimanus are estimated to reach around 9 meters in length.
This animal possessed forefins and hindfins that were roughly equal in length, narrow, and elongated.
Temnodontosaurus species were large animals, reaching up to 12 meters in length, with great muscular strength and were skilled coastal predators.
While the full body color of Temnodontosaurus is unknown, a specimen of T. trigonodon showed dark coloration on its forefins, suggesting some ichthyosaurs were uniformly dark.
A possible specimen of T. trigonodon found in January 2021 in Rutland Water is estimated to be slightly over 10 meters long.

In 1922, von Huene described imposing vertebrae from the Banz Abbey Museum, with the largest measuring 22 cm in height. Based on a nearly complete skeleton of T. trigonodon, McGowan estimated the size of von Huene's Banz specimen at 16 meters long.
Researchers suggest the serrated chondroderms on the flipper may have acted as noise-cancelling structures to help Temnodontosaurus hunt stealthily at night.

The first known fossil of Temnodontosaurus was a complete skull and partial skeleton found by Joseph and Mary Anning in the early 1810s in Dorset, England. Joseph Anning discovered the first Temnodontosaurus skull around 1810 on the cliffs of Black Ven in Dorset, England.
Carl von Theodori described the species T. trigonodon in 1843 based on a colossal specimen found in Holzmaden, Germany.
Friedrich von Huene described the species L. nürtingensis in 1931 based on a specimen found in a quarry in Nürtingen, Germany.

A fragmentary Temnodontosaurus specimen was discovered in the Atacama Desert, Chile, in 1988. The Chilean Temnodontosaurus specimen comes from the La Negra Formation, which dates to the Early Jurassic.
A life-size concrete sculpture of Temnodontosaurus created by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins between 1852 and 1854 was displayed at Crystal Palace Park in London.
Temnodontosaurus utilized a thunniform swimming method, evolving away from the anguilliform (eel-like) swimming of earlier species.
As warm-blooded animals with high metabolic rates, ichthyosaurs like Temnodontosaurus were active swimmers.
Temnodontosaurus likely had great visual capacity due to a high number of photoreceptor cells in its eyes.
Evidence from stomach contents proves Temnodontosaurus was an apex predator whose diet consisted mainly of molluscs.
Fossil evidence shows that Temnodontosaurus engaged in aggressive combat, with several specimens bearing healed injuries from other large marine reptiles.
The size of the teeth that caused the wounds suggests that the jaw tissues of Temnodontosaurus were very thin.
Temnodontosaurus were large, very resistant swimmers capable of diving to deep zones of Jurassic seas to catch prey.
Temnodontosaurus is a basal and the largest representative of the parvipelvian subgroup of ichthyosaurs.
Michael W. Maisch transferred the species to the genus Temnodontosaurus in 1998, including specimens from Germany and France.
Maisch and Hungerbühler argued in 1997 that the holotype of L. nürtingensis is well-preserved and should be attributed to Temnodontosaurus.
McGowan and Motani classified the species as a nomen dubium in 2003, though later studies maintained its validity and genus assignment.
McGowan redescribed the Lyme Regis skull as the holotype of the new species T. eurycephalus. The specific name eurycephalus means "broad head", referring to the taxon's cranial morphology.
Temnodontosaurus lived during the Lower Hettangian to Toarcian stages of the Jurassic period.
Temnodontosaurus lived between 198 and 185 million years ago (Hettangian to Toarcian) in what is now Europe, specifically England and Germany.
Phylogenetic analyses and diagnostic problems suggest that Temnodontosaurus is currently a polyphyletic taxon requiring revision.
A 2023 study suggests that the holotype of T. trigonodon differs significantly from other assigned specimens, requiring future re-evaluation of the diagnosis.
Authors of the 2022 T. zetlandicus study noted that T. azerguensis and T. eurycephalus are too phylogenetically unstable for a monophyletic Temnodontosaurus grouping.
